# Task mapping

Every correspondence between the tasks in the Catalog and the task entries in the
Cognitive Atlas, in both directions: a summary of each direction by match type, then the
full row tables. The [Atlas mapping method](../methods/atlas_mapping_method.md) page
explains what the match types mean and how each row was decided, and
[The Catalog vs the Atlas](the_catalog_vs_the_atlas.md) says what the correspondence
adds up to.

The source of record is `data/mappings/`, not this page. Atlas entry names are
reproduced exactly as the API returns them. A few carry a curly apostrophe or an en
dash, and one (`Penn` + a mis-encoded apostrophe + `s Logical Reasoning Test`) carries a
double-encoding defect present in the Atlas itself. These are left uncorrected so that a
name here matches the source byte for byte.

## Atlas to Catalog, entries with no counterpart

Most Atlas entries have no counterpart here, which is expected rather than a gap: the
Catalog admits only event-producing experimental paradigms, while the Atlas mixes those
with instruments of several other kinds.

```{include} ../_generated/mapping_task_reverse_scope.md
```

The kind assigned to an unmatched entry is derived from its name by rule and is a
heuristic, not a hand-checked judgement, so treat the grouping below as an aid to
navigation rather than a classification. The `none` verdict itself was reviewed.

```{include} ../_generated/atlas_task_unmatched.md
```

## Reading the two directions together

The directions answer different questions and can differ without contradiction. The
Catalog-to-Atlas table asks whether the Atlas contains a given paradigm; the
Atlas-to-Catalog table asks, for each Atlas entry, whether the Catalog covers it.

Three tasks are `none` in the first table yet appear in the second with `related` rows:
Self-Paced Reading, Sentence Comprehension and Virtual Radial Arm Maze. The Atlas has
no entry that *is* any of those paradigms, but it does hold adjacent entries
(`Eye tracking paradigms`, `syntactic task`, `Porteus maze test`). Both statements are
true.
